one_liner: Reference code for CSR5, a tiled CSR variant for SpMV that beat MKL, cuSPARSE, CUSP and pOSKI on irregular matrices in 2015.
what_it_does: Converts an existing CSR matrix (row_ptr, col_idx, values) in place into CSR5, which adds a tile pointer and a tile descriptor array (about 2% extra space), then runs y = alpha*A*x on it. There are separate header-only code drops for AVX2 CPUs, KNC Xeon Phi, KNL (AVX-512), CUDA and OpenCL (AMD and NVIDIA). Each exposes the same small handle API (inputCSR, setX, asCSR5, spmv, asCSR, destroy). It is a research benchmark rather than a packaged library, and it does not replace a BLAS or sparse-library call directly.
how_it_is_fast: Nonzeros are cut into fixed-size 2D tiles of omega columns (the SIMD or warp width) by sigma rows (chosen from the matrix's average nonzeros per row and the cache). Each tile gets a bit-flag descriptor of row starts, so every SIMD lane does the same amount of work no matter how uneven the row lengths are. Partial row sums are combined with a redesigned segmented sum that is mostly a prefix-sum scan, and a calibrator array fixes rows that span tiles. Load balance comes from the nonzero count, not the row count, so power-law and other irregular matrices do not leave lanes idle.
when_to_use: Repeated double-precision SpMV on irregular matrices (power-law graphs, web, circuit) where row-length skew hurts CSR kernels
Iterative solvers with tens or more iterations: the paper says conversion costs about as much as a few SpMVs and that CSR5 was the only format beating CSR at 50 iterations
GPU SpMV (CUDA or OpenCL) where you want one format that copes with both regular and irregular sparsity
As a reference design to port into your own sparse kernel library under MIT terms
when_not_to_use: Regular, well-balanced matrices on Intel CPUs: the paper says MKL had the best CPU average on the regular set, and on Xeon Phi CSR5 lost to ESB and MKL there
Single-shot SpMV, where the CSR->CSR5 conversion is not amortized

When you need a maintained, packaged library: no commits since Dec 2020, the code is per-platform folders built from Makefiles, and the 2015-era baselines (MKL 11.2, cuSPARSE 6.5) have been improved since
Single precision on CPU or Phi: the AVX2, KNC and KNL versions support only double; float exists only in the CUDA and OpenCL versions
Other kernels (SpMM, SpGEMM, transpose-multiply): this repo does SpMV only

integration.dependencies: OpenMP and AVX2 intrinsics (CPU); CUDA toolkit (CUDA version); OpenCL 1.2 runtime (OpenCL versions); Intel compiler suggested for Phi/KNL
integration.min_toolchain: C++ compiler with OpenMP and AVX2 (Makefile: -O3 -mavx -mavx2 -march=native -fopenmp); README tested Intel C/C++ 2015; CUDA 6.5-era
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2; Xeon Phi KNC; KNL AVX-512; NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA/OpenCL); AMD GPUs (OpenCL)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the handle stores raw pointers to caller arrays and mutates them, so one handle per matrix and no concurrent use
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it takes standard CSR arrays as input, but you must keep a handle, convert, and call its own spmv(alpha, y) instead of mkl_sparse_d_mv or cusparseSpMV

gotchas: asCSR5() transposes the caller's col_idx and values arrays in place; they are not valid CSR again until you call asCSR() or destroy().
spmv() returns ANONYMOUSLIB_UNSUPPORTED_CSR_SPMV if the handle has not been converted to CSR5 first.
The bundled main.cpp times only CSR5 against a single-thread naive loop and checks results with a 1% relative tolerance; it does not rerun the MKL/cuSPARSE comparisons from the paper.
The README's change log records later fixes to the AVX2 and Phi versions (a small-matrix bug and y-update performance, Jul 2016) and a CUDA timing bug (Apr 2016), all after the ICS 2015 numbers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Ginkgo is a maintained solver library with its own SpMV formats, so prefer it for production; pick CSR5 when you need to study or port a load-balanced SpMV kernel for irregular matrices. Sympiler and the A64FX CHOLMOD work target direct factorization, not SpMV.
verified_claims_summary: Peer-reviewed ICS 2015 paper: in double-precision SpMV on 10 irregular matrices, CSR5 averaged 17.6% over the best prior method on dual Xeon E5-2667 v3 (pOSKI there, not MKL), 28.5% on GTX 980, 173.0% on R9 290X and 293.3% on Xeon Phi 5110p, with peaks of 213.3/153.6/405.1/943.3%. On 14 regular matrices it was 'comparable or better', but MKL had the best CPU average. Compilers were Intel C/C++ 15.0.1, g++ 4.8.2 and CUDA 6.5; the paper gives no flags.
status_note: Abandoned since Dec 2020, but MIT-licensed, header-only per platform, and small enough to vendor or port; expect to modernize the CUDA and OpenCL build files and to re-benchmark against current MKL and cuSPARSE before adopting.
